outcome: Still open as far as the sources show: no proof or disproof of the infinitude of Mersenne primes (or of even perfect numbers) has been accepted since 26 January 2024. The events are two mutually contradictory unrefereed 2024 claims (Vega: finitely many; a Preprints.org note: infinitely many), the discovery of the 52nd known Mersenne prime 2¹³⁶²⁷⁹⁸⁴¹ − 1 in October 2024 (an instance, not a bearing on infinitude), GIMPS verification milestones in 2026, and heuristic, statistical or unrelated papers that do not settle the question.
problem_asks: (1) Are there infinitely many Mersenne primes, i.e. infinitely many primes of the form 2ᵖ − 1 (equivalently, infinitely many prime exponents p for which 2ᵖ − 1 is prime)? (2) Stated as equivalent: are there infinitely many even perfect numbers? By Euclid–Euler, even perfect numbers correspond one-to-one with Mersenne primes, so part (2) stands or falls with part (1). The bullet names the Lenstra–Pomerance–Wagstaff conjecture as the source of the question. The bullet itself asks only the yes/no question of infinitude. It does not ask for the conjecture's predicted asymptotic count (about e^γ/log 2 · log log x Mersenne primes below x) or its growth law. It asks for neither a bound nor a count.

events.what_happened: Budee U Zaman, 'Infinite Primes, Quadratic Polynomials, and Fermat's Criterion', EasyChair Preprint 11402, dated 28 November 2023. The abstract asks whether 4(Mₚ − 2)² + 1 gives infinitely many primes, proposes Fermat primes as a criterion, and states: 'Furthermore, we present a basic argument demonstrating the infinity of Mersenne primes.' The argument itself was not visible in the abstract I retrieved.
events.delivers: As claimed in the abstract: infinitely many Mersenne primes, by a 'basic argument' that I could not read. The rest of the paper concerns a hypothesis (the Fermat-prime criterion) and a partial result for primes of the form x² + 1.
events.remains: Nothing is established in the abstract I could read. If the basic argument is valid, it would leave no part of problem_asks open, but I could not check it.
events.doubts: EasyChair preprint; the page says nothing about peer review or journal publication. The infinitude claim is one sentence in the abstract. The author's other preprints (Collatz, twin primes, 'natural number infinite formula') are not reviewed here. No engagement with this claim found.
events.direction: Asserts the positive answer (infinitely many Mersenne primes, hence infinitely many even perfect numbers), as a claim in one sentence of the abstract.

events.what_happened: Frank Vega, 'Note for the Perfect Numbers'. Listed on Cambridge Engage with posting date 22 April 2024 (Version 1, Working Paper), and on EasyChair as Preprint 13131 with versions dated 29 April 2024 (v1), 11 July (v2), 12 July (v3) and 15 July 2024 (v4, current). Abstract, as shown on the EasyChair pages: 'the infinitude of Mersenne primes remains an open question'; 'If there are finitely many Mersenne primes, then there would also be a finite number of even perfect numbers'; then 'showing that there are finitely many Mersenne primes, we provide a partial answer by proving that is false the infinitude of even perfect numbers.' The version notes say v2 fixed a sentence about consecutive Mersenne numbers, v3 summarised an explanation involving a geometric series, and v4 fixed a formula in Proposition 1. The full PDF could not be retrieved (EasyChair download routes returned 404), so the argument was not read.
events.revisions: Cambridge listing: posting date 22 April 2024 (v1). EasyChair: v1 29 April 2024; v2 11 July 2024; v3 12 July 2024; v4 15 July 2024. The two dates for v1 differ; the earlier date is used.
events.delivers: As claimed (abstract only): finitely many Mersenne primes, and therefore finitely many even perfect numbers, via the standard Euclid–Euler correspondence. No restriction on the claim is stated. Whether the finiteness argument holds is not established by anything I could read.
events.remains: Nothing is left open on the claim as stated, if it holds. The claim is unverified, and the abstract itself calls the infinitude question open.
events.doubts: (1) Venue: an EasyChair preprint. The Cambridge Engage listing says it 'has not been peer-reviewed by Cambridge University Press' and is a Working Paper. No journal version was found. (2) The abstract calls the Mersenne question open and, in the same abstract, claims a 'partial answer' that settles it. (3) It asserts the answer opposite to the heuristic expectation (Lenstra–Pomerance–Wagstaff predict infinitely many). That is a reason for extra scrutiny, not a refutation. (4) Revisions changed a sentence, a formula and a summary, and the version notes record no change to the main claim and no external objection. (5) The same author's companion Cambridge note (22 April 2024) assumes infinitude instead. (6) I could not read the argument, so I cannot say where the key step (the geometric series argument) holds or fails. No refutation or endorsement was found in any search.
events.direction: The opposite of the expected answer: claims finitely many Mersenne primes, and so finitely many even perfect numbers.

events.what_happened: Frank Vega, 'Note for the Mersenne Primes', on Cambridge Engage, posting date 22 April 2024 (Version 1, Working Paper). Abstract: 'under the assumption that there are infinitely many Mersenne primes', the author proves that odd perfect numbers do not exist, using elementary techniques and properties of the sigma function.
events.delivers: A conditional result about odd perfect numbers, given infinitely many Mersenne primes as a hypothesis. It does not establish infinitude, and it is about a different problem.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. This event takes the positive answer to part (1) as a hypothesis.
events.doubts: Not peer-reviewed per the Cambridge listing. It is conditional on the open question. Its author also posted the opposite assumption (finitely many Mersenne primes) in the event above. The odd-perfect argument was not examined.
events.direction: Conditional on the positive answer; concludes about odd perfect numbers, which the bullet does not ask.

events.what_happened: 'Hyperbolic Primality Test and Catalan–Mersenne Number Conjecture', Preprints.org manuscript 202405.0952, submitted 10 May 2024 and posted 14 May 2024, not peer-reviewed. The page returned 403, so this is from search excerpts only. The excerpts say it develops a primality test for Mersenne numbers, argues that the 5th Catalan–Mersenne number is prime, and claims this 'demonstrat[es] the infinitude of Mersenne primes'. A lemma states there are infinitely many Mersenne primes; the argument relies on a theorem that if there is one double Mersenne prime, it generates an infinite series of Mersenne primes, and cites M₇ as such a prime. The excerpts do not show a proof of that theorem.
events.delivers: As claimed in excerpts: infinitely many Mersenne primes. The generating step is not visible in what I could read. The claim also rests on the 5th Catalan–Mersenne number being prime, which by itself gives one prime and no infinitude.
events.remains: If the generating theorem holds, nothing; the claim depends on a step I could not read. Otherwise all of problem_asks.
events.doubts: (1) Preprints.org marks it not peer-reviewed. (2) The infinitude conclusion depends on a generating theorem, and no proof of it appears in any excerpt I could see. (3) From the excerpt, the lemma and its proof appear to run in opposite directions: the lemma says a non-trivial solution implies primality, while the proof says a lattice point on the hyperbola makes Mₚ not prime. This is my reading of a search excerpt and has not been checked against the full text. (4) Showing one Catalan–Mersenne number is prime cannot by itself give infinitude. (5) The author is not identified in any source I could open.
events.direction: The positive answer: infinitely many Mersenne primes, and so infinitely many even perfect numbers.
people: Author not identified (the author list was not in any excerpt; the page returned 403)

events.what_happened: Luke Durant's GPU-based run for the Great Internet Mersenne Prime Search found the prime 2¹³⁶²⁷⁹⁸⁴¹ − 1 (exponent 136279841, 41,024,320 decimal digits). GIMPS's milestone log records 'Prime M(136279841) discovered!' dated 12 October 2024. John D. Cook's post of 21 October 2024 reports the announcement ('A new Mersenne prime discovery was announced today'), notes it is confirmed prime, and says it 'may not be the 52nd Mersenne prime' because gaps are not yet excluded. mersenne.org lists it as 52nd, marked provisional.
events.revisions: GIMPS milestone (discovery) 12 Oct 2024; public announcement 21 Oct 2024 (press and blog). The first public written record found is the 12 Oct milestone entry.
events.delivers: Adds one more Mersenne prime (the largest known) to the list of known ones. It is an instance of the set the problem asks about. It bears on counts and records, not on whether the set is infinite.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. The event does not bear on whether there are infinitely many Mersenne primes.

checked_by.who: GIMPS (Great Internet Mersenne Prime Search) volunteer computation, with independent re-runs
checked_by.qualification: Computational primality testing (Lucas–Lehmer and Fermat tests). Not a human reading of mathematics.
checked_by.what_they_did: Flagged by a Fermat probable-prime test, confirmed by a Lucas–Lehmer test, then verified on other systems (per heise and press coverage, not opened)

machine_checked.system: GIMPS Lucas–Lehmer test (computer verification; not a proof assistant)

events.directly_checkable: The exponent 136279841 can be checked by running the Lucas–Lehmer test on 2¹³⁶²⁷⁹⁸⁴¹ − 1. It is deterministic and very expensive, which is why GIMPS used GPUs.
events.doubts: No doubt about the prime itself. A count caveat: mersenne.org says the ranking is provisional, because 'not all candidates between M82589933 and M136279841 have been eliminated'. That affects where this prime sits in the count, not whether it is a Mersenne prime.
events.direction: Neutral to the question. It confirms one more exponent for which 2ᵖ − 1 is prime.
events.object: The prime 2¹³⁶²⁷⁹⁸⁴¹ − 1 itself, with 41,024,320 decimal digits. It is explicit (a specific number), and its primality is certified by the Lucas–Lehmer test. It is not a non-constructive existence result, and it is not a counterexample to anything.

events.what_happened: Preprints.org manuscript 202410.0547, 'A Note on Odd Perfect Numbers', submitted 10 July 2025 and posted 14 July 2025 (from search excerpt; the page returned 403). Its abstract claims to prove that no odd perfect numbers exist, by contradiction using σ(N) and φ(N)/N. The author is not shown in the excerpt. A separate EasyChair series by Frank Vega on odd perfect numbers (2022 onward, conditional on the Riemann Hypothesis) is a different record and was not opened.
events.delivers: As claimed in the excerpt: no odd perfect numbers. This is a neighbouring problem, not the bullet's question, and it does not bear on the infinitude of even perfect numbers.
events.doubts: Marked not peer-reviewed. The argument was not read, so its key inequalities are unchecked.
events.direction: Neighbouring: a negative answer to the odd perfect number question, which the bullet does not ask.

events.what_happened: Moustafa Ibrahim, 'The emergence of the Mersenne Star: a new geometry of prime numbers bridging physics and artificial general intelligence', Arab Journal of Basic and Applied Sciences (2025), per the PhilArchive record (IBRTEO-8; the page returned 403, so this is from the search listing). It proposes a geometric shape derived from a 'Quanta Prime Sequence' and suggests that intelligent computer systems could detect primes by recognising such patterns ('Artificial Prime Intelligence').
events.delivers: Nothing on infinitude. A geometric observation about primes and a speculative research direction, with no proof claimed in the excerpt.
events.doubts: The proposal that intelligent systems may detect primes is speculative. No test or replication was found, and the full text was not read.
events.direction: Neutral: no claim about the question.

events.what_happened: Michael Mark Anthony, 'Infinitude Condition for Mersenne and Sophie Germain Primes', Preprints.org, DOI 10.20944/preprints202510.1280.v1, posted 16 October 2025 (from search listing; the DOI redirects to a page that returned 403). Per the excerpt, it is not peer-reviewed. It begins by noting that it is not known whether there are infinitely many Mersenne primes, and it uses trigonometric identities and cotangent sum-of-divisors identities to argue for a 'structural result'. The excerpt is cut off before the claimed 'infinitude condition' is stated.
events.delivers: Unknown: the result it claims was not visible. Per the excerpt it does not claim to settle infinitude outright.
events.remains: Unknown from what I could read.
events.doubts: Not peer-reviewed per the listing. The claimed condition could not be read, so there is nothing specific to evaluate. Later-work status: this paper itself treats infinitude as open.
events.direction: Unknown: the claimed condition was not visible.

events.what_happened: Mihai Prunescu, 'Arithmetic closed forms count the Mersenne primes, the Fermat primes and the twin-prime pairs', arXiv (math.NT), submitted 1 December 2025, single version. The abstract says the closed forms count all Mersenne primes between 0 and 2^(n+2) − 1, each a fixed finite composition of addition, subtraction, multiplication, division with remainder and 2ⁿ, and names the Lucas–Lehmer and Pépin tests for the counting forms.
events.delivers: Bounded counts of Mersenne primes below 2ⁿ⁺² − 1, per the abstract. A bounded count cannot settle whether an infinite set is infinite.
events.doubts: The abstract is ambiguous: it describes the forms as finite arithmetic compositions, yet names primality tests for the counting forms. It does not say whether the forms encode computed data. The body was not read.
events.direction: Neutral: bounded counts; no infinitude claim.

events.what_happened: Tyler Ross, 'A Perfect Number Generalization and Some Euclid-Euler Type Results', arXiv:2512.04417 (math.NT), submitted 4 December 2025, single version. Introduces S-perfect numbers (integers equal to a weighted sum of their proper divisors, with weights from a fixed set S). Shows there are infinitely many {0, m}- and {−1, m}-perfect numbers for every m ≥ 1, and characterises the {−1, m}-perfect numbers of the form 2ᵏp and all even {−1, 1}-perfect numbers. The page says nothing on whether there are infinitely many even or odd perfect numbers. The journal reference listed (J. Int. Seq. 27 (2024), Article 24.7.5) conflicts with the December 2025 submission date.
events.revisions: One version (v1, 4 Dec 2025). Journal reference listed as 2024, which conflicts with the arXiv date.
events.delivers: Infinitely many perfect numbers of the generalised S-type for the stated weight sets. It is about a different question: the classical even perfect numbers and their infinitude are not addressed.
events.direction: Neutral: an infinitude result for a generalised notion, about a different question.

events.what_happened: Samuel S. Wagstaff Jr. (Purdue), 'Two Mersenne Prime Conjectures', Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.2. Received 1 September 2025, revised 27 September 2025, published 4 December 2025. Abstract: 'We discuss two conjectures about Mersenne numbers, an old one and a new one. Heuristic arguments support both conjectures.' The introduction describes the old one as the 1989 'new Mersenne conjecture' of Bateman, Selfridge and Wagstaff, and the new one as a 2025 conjecture. The author's copy (homes.cerias.purdue.edu) is titled with 'Chen's Mersenne Conjecture of 2025' in its outline, but its statement was not readable.
events.revisions: Journal publication 4 Dec 2025. Whether an earlier preprint existed was not checked, so this may be later than the first public written version.
events.delivers: No proof. Heuristic support for two conjectures about Mersenne numbers. As far as I could read, neither is stated as settling infinitude.
events.remains: Infinitude, as far as I could tell. Whether the 2025 conjecture bears on infinitude is unknown, because its statement was not readable.

checked_by.who: Journal of Integer Sequences (a peer-reviewed journal)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the article after its standard process. I did not inspect referee reports.

events.doubts: Heuristic only, by its own abstract. The 2025 conjecture's statement was not read, so I cannot say whether it asserts or denies infinitude.
events.direction: Neutral: heuristic support for two conjectures about Mersenne numbers. It does not answer the question.

events.what_happened: Jesus Dominguez, 'Arithmetic Bias in the Distribution of Mersenne Prime Exponents and the Divisor Structure of p−1', arXiv:2603.08994. v1 submitted 9 March 2026; seven versions, the latest 4 October 2026. Statistical study: known Mersenne-prime exponents p ≥ 13 show systematically elevated values of S(p) = log τ(p−1)/log log p compared with nearby prime exponents. The author describes the effect as moderate, with no analytic explanation.
events.revisions: v1 9 Mar 2026; v2 14 Mar; v3 31 May; v4 2 Jun; v5 30 Jul; v6 28 Sep; v7 4 Oct 2026
events.delivers: A statistical pattern in the distribution of known Mersenne-prime exponents. Nothing on infinitude.
events.doubts: A statistical pattern in a finite sample of known exponents. The abstract says transmission to primality is heuristic.
events.direction: Neutral: a distributional observation about known exponents.

events.what_happened: JohnK Wright V, 'Predicting Mersenne Prime Exponents Using Euler's Quadratic Polynomial C(n) = n² + n + 41 with Nearest-Integer Rounding', arXiv:2603.06579. The arXiv identifier indicates March 2026, but the record I retrieved gave a submission date of 17 December 2025. The conflict is unresolved, so the month is taken from the identifier. Proposes a 'Wright–Euler Mersenne Exponent Hypothesis' for candidate exponents, and reports seven exact matches and four close approximations among 43 known exponents (indices 10 to 52).
events.revisions: Retrieved record shows one version; its date (17 Dec 2025) conflicts with the arXiv identifier (2603, i.e. March 2026).
events.delivers: A heuristic rule for candidate exponents. Nothing on infinitude.
events.doubts: Single author and unrefereed. The rule was fitted, then tested on 43 exponents, with about 560 candidates and about 50 prime outputs. Seven exact matches from that many candidates is weak evidence, by the abstract's own numbers.
events.direction: Neutral: a candidate-exponent hypothesis, not about infinitude.

events.what_happened: Matthew Baker, 'The sesquicentennial of the prime number 2¹²⁷ − 1', arXiv:2608.05319, submitted 5 August 2026, single version. Marks 150 years since Lucas's 1876 proof that 2¹²⁷ − 1 is prime, reviews that history, and gives a modern proof of the Lucas–Lehmer test. Its body says 'it is unknown whether there are infinitely many such primes' (from the Lucas–Lehmer section; the sentence is cut in my retrieval). Acknowledgements, from the arXiv HTML (v1): 'and ChatGPT 5.4 for assistance with proofreading and polishing the prose.' Not load-bearing on the mathematics, so ChatGPT 5.4 is not listed as a system.
events.delivers: A historical review and a modern proof of the Lucas–Lehmer test, which is a criterion for one exponent at a time. No infinitude result.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. The paper itself states infinitude is unknown.
events.direction: Neutral on the question. It states, in its body, that infinitude is unknown.

events.what_happened: GIMPS milestone log records 'All tests below M(82589933) verified, officially making it the 51st Mersenne prime' on 4 September 2026. Earlier milestones: 49th (M(74207281)) official on 23 June 2025 and 50th (M(77232917)) on 8 September 2025. mersenne.org's table lists 52 entries, and marks M136279841 provisional: 'not all candidates between M82589933 and M136279841 have been eliminated'. The page does not state a total count.
events.delivers: Verification of all exponents below M(82589933), confirming the 51st ranking. It fixes part of the count of known Mersenne primes. It says nothing about whether the set is infinite.

checked_by.what_they_did: Re-ran tests so all exponents below the bound were covered; recorded as an official milestone

events.doubts: The 52nd ranking is provisional. Wikipedia's count of 52 'as of 2025' predates this milestone. See disputes.
events.direction: Neutral: count-related. No bearing on infinitude.

disputes.summary: Two unrefereed 2024 claims give opposite answers. Vega's 'Note for the Perfect Numbers' claims finitely many Mersenne primes (and so finitely many even perfect numbers). The Preprints.org note 202405.0952 claims infinitely many. Neither has been engaged with publicly in what I found, and neither is adjudicated here.

The count of known Mersenne primes is disputed in the sources. Wikipedia's article gives 52 'as of 2025'. mersenne.org lists 52 with the 52nd marked provisional, and verifies only up to the 51st (4 September 2026). The 2024 blog post says the new prime 'may not be the 52nd'.

The discovery date of 2¹³⁶²⁷⁹⁸⁴¹ − 1 is 12 October 2024 in the GIMPS milestone log, but press and blog coverage date the announcement to 21 October 2024. The record uses 12 October, the first public written record found.

summary: About 45 searches (listed below) and about 30 pages opened. Around 10 publisher and repository pages returned 403 or 404, and I say per item where a claim is known only from a search excerpt. No proof or disproof of the infinitude of Mersenne primes, and so no settlement of the even-perfect-number form, was accepted in the window from 26 January 2024 to 11 October 2026. Sources that treat the question as open include Wikipedia's current article (lists it as unsolved, and says it is not even known whether the set is finite or infinite), Baker's August 2026 arXiv paper (body: 'it is unknown whether there are infinitely many such primes'), and Wagstaff's 2025 journal paper (heuristic support for two conjectures, no proof). The substantive events are the two contradictory 2024 claims. The Vega note (22 April 2024; EasyChair versions to 15 July 2024) asserts finiteness and abstracts that call the Mersenne question open in the same breath. I could not read its argument, because the full-text routes returned 404, so I cannot say whether the key step holds. The Preprints.org note (14 May 2024) asserts infinitude through a generating theorem I could not see. The pre-window Zaman EasyChair (November 2023) asserts infinitude in one sentence and is recorded as predating the window. The only new mathematical fact in the window is the 52nd known Mersenne prime (12 October 2024), an instance of the set that bears on counts, not infinitude. Other 2025–2026 papers (Prunescu, Ross, Wagstaff, Domínguez, Wright, Anthony) do not settle the question, though Anthony's excerpt was cut before its claim. Several 2026 claims of progress that I checked were in the wrong area: OpenAI's ten-advances list has no Mersenne or perfect-number item, and the Axiom formalisation is about prime gaps. Two Emergent Mind citations are wrong: arXiv 2608.30196 is a paper on Cayley maps, and the open-status quotes it attributes to Pengelley (2502.11165) and Dilcher–Ericksen (2509.03147) were not in any readable text I could retrieve. Several ResearchGate titles (for example 'Proof of the existence of infinite number of Mersenne primes', publication 381215076) were seen only in search results; they were blocked, and their authors and dates are unknown, so they are not recorded as events and are listed in incomplete. On AI: no AI system is named in any source that bears on infinitude or on the even-perfect-number form. The only AI-related item in the Mersenne literature is Baker's acknowledgement crediting 'ChatGPT 5.4' with proofreading and polishing prose, which is not load-bearing, so no system entry is made and the event is recorded with none_found false. The GIMPS discovery used GPUs as hardware for GIMPS software, not an AI system. The Mersenne Star paper (Ibrahim, 2025) proposes that intelligent systems might detect primes in future and reports no system doing mathematics. AI searches covered AlphaEvolve, AlphaProof, Deep Think, GPT-5 and Gemini/Claude/ChatGPT claims about Mersenne primes; Tao's AI-contributions wiki (last updated 30 June 2026; the page as fetched names no Mersenne or perfect-number problem); Erdős-problem AI results; and Lean/mathlib. None turned up a Mersenne or perfect-number result attributed to an AI. The Lean side has no infinitude formalisation; mathlib has Euclid's direction of Euclid–Euler (archive/100-theorems-list/70_perfect_numbers), which concerns perfect numbers rather than infinitude, and I did not pin its date, so it is not recorded as an event.
competing_reading: A reader could treat the Vega note as a serious attempt at a 'no' answer (finitely many), and so as a live resolution of the bullet. Against this, the note is unrefereed, the abstract itself calls the question open, and it contradicts the heuristic expectation. A reader could also treat the 14 May 2024 Preprints.org note as a proof-claim of infinitude, but its generating step was not visible to me. A third reading counts the 2024 discovery of M136279841 as progress on the problem, because it adds a member of the set. Under the scope rule in §2.1, an added instance of an existential family does not move the infinitude question, so I have not treated it as progress; a reader who counts instances will reach a different event list.
what_would_settle_it: For the Vega note: the full text and a refereed or expert verdict on the finiteness step, or a published refutation. For the Preprints.org 202405.0952 note: its full text (lemma and generating theorem), its author list, and any verdict. For the question as a whole: a refereed proof either way. Until then the best-supported status is 'open'. Also needed: the full text of Anthony (202510.1280), the 2025 'Chen' conjecture in Wagstaff's paper, and the ResearchGate items, to rule them in or out as events.
